analysis.one_liner: Blocks brand-name drug makers from using safety-program patents to delay generic competition.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate committee it was referred to.
analysis.plain_summary: When the FDA requires a brand-name drug to have a safety program (a REMS), the brand maker sometimes holds patents on parts of that safety program and uses them in court to keep cheaper generic versions off the market for years. This bill says those patents can't delay a generic's approval, and that the brand maker could only sue for money damages — not win a court order blocking the generic. The bill was introduced with bipartisan sponsorship but never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take drugs with FDA safety programs, since faster generic entry means lower prices, and generic drug makers who would face fewer lawsuits blocking their approvals.

how_it_helps.text: A generic maker's certification that a patent covering a REMS safety-program element is invalid or not infringed would no longer delay FDA approval of the generic, removing a common holdup tactic.
The bill applies retroactively to generic applications already submitted, so drugs stuck in litigation could move sooner.
In patent suits over REMS requirements, the brand-name sponsor could seek only money damages, not a court injunction shutting the generic out of the market while litigation drags on.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers would lose a tool that extends their exclusive sales period beyond the main patent, giving up years of higher-priced sales on certain drugs.

drawbacks.text: Weakening the 30-month patent-litigation stay and limiting remedies to damages could let generics launch while their patents are still being litigated, and brand makers argue this reduces the incentive to invest in developing drugs that require costly safety programs.
Brand makers could still face uncertainty over which REMS-related patents and trade secrets are covered, inviting new litigation over the rule's boundaries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the subset of drugs with FDA-mandated safety programs, faster generic entry would likely mean meaningful price savings for patients, at the cost of somewhat weaker patent remedies for brand makers on safety-program features only — not on the drugs' core patents. The scope is narrow, so the public benefit is real but limited.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Maggie Hassan introduced the bill on September 22, 2022, joined by Republican Sen. Mike Braun.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the record before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers keep the ability to use safety-program patents and injunctions to delay generic competition, preserving years of extended exclusive sales on affected drugs.

for.name: Sen. Maggie Hassan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar REMS-related patents from delaying generic drug approvals.

for.name: Sen. Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing or markup — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic lead sponsor and its sole cosponsor was a Republican, but with only one cosponsor it never advanced far enough for any party-split vote.

industries.note: The bill would strip a tactic — patents on FDA safety-program elements plus injunction lawsuits — that keeps generics off the market longer, costing makers years of monopoly-priced sales on certain drugs.
Generic approvals could take effect without delays from REMS-related patent certifications or injunctions, letting generics reach patients sooner.
